title: Unique test data and dynamic locators

parts.title: TypeScript for building a unique value at runtime

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - TypeScript - Building a unique value at runtime

By the end of this lesson you will build a guaranteed-different string on every run
using `+` and `Math.random()` — the exact technique [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2) uses so two
runs of the same test never collide.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `+` on strings | building a unique value, and a dynamic XPath string |
| 2 | `Math.random()` | the source of the "unique" part |

## 1. The `+` operator on strings

`+` concatenates two strings into one. A number gets converted to text first, rather
than mixing silently.

**Expected:** `Learner42`, `Learner 42`, `Learner42`.

Nothing in this course uses template literals (`` `${}` ``) yet — that's a later day.
`+` is the whole toolkit for now.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same operator, different pieces: build one sentence out of three separate `const` strings, with the spaces in the right places. Then print `typeof ("id" + 42)` and confirm for yourself that the result is a string, not a number.

blocks.text:
## 2. `Math.random()`

Returns a float, always `0 <= x < 1` — never negative, never exactly 1. On its own it's
not a usable id; you convert or slice it into something readable.

console.log(Math.random()); // e.g. 0.7392... — different every run
console.log(Math.random().toString(36)); // base-36: digits + letters, e.g. "0.k3j9f2..."
console.log(Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)); // drop the "0." prefix, keep 6 chars

**Expected:** three lines, all different on every run you make — that unpredictability
is exactly what makes it useful for uniqueness. `.toString(36)` turns the float into
letters+digits instead of a long decimal.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same generator, a shorter slice: keep 4 characters instead of 6, and print the length to prove you got 4. Run the cell three or four times and watch the value change each time — that unpredictability is the whole feature.

blocks.text:
## 3. Putting them together

```ts
const unique = "learner" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8);
```

Where you'll use this next: `"//input[@value='" + unique + "']"` — Day 3.2 builds an
XPath string the same way, by concatenating a runtime value into a fixed template.

**Expected:** a string starting with `learner`, followed by 6 random characters; then
that same string embedded inside an XPath expression.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same technique, a different template: build a unique username and embed it in a CSS selector string (`"input[name='" + unique + "']"`) instead of an XPath one. Print both the value and the finished selector — string-building does not care which locator syntax it is feeding.

blocks.text:
## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `+` on strings | concatenates; numbers get converted to text first |
| `Math.random()` | always `0 <= x < 1`; slice/convert it into something readable |
| Combining them | `"prefix" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)` — a fresh value every run |

**Next:** [Day 3.2 — Unique test data and dynamic locators](/learn/w2/d3/p2)
What can `Math.random()` return?

options: Any float from 0 up to but not including 1
Any float from 0 up to and including 1
Any float, including negative ones
checkpoint.explanation: `0 <= x < 1` — never negative, and never exactly 1. On its own it is not a usable id, which is why the lesson runs it through `.toString(36).slice(2, 8)` to get something short and readable.

blocks.text: `console.log("Learner" + 42)` prints what?

options: `Learner 42` — `+` inserts a separator between the two
`Learner42` — the number is converted to text first
A type error — you cannot add a number to a string
checkpoint.explanation: `+` converts the number to `"42"` and joins them with nothing in between. No space appears unless you add one yourself, which is the mistake that shows up as `Learner42` where `Learner 42` was wanted.

parts.title: Unique test data and dynamic locators

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - Fundamentals - Unique test data and dynamic locators

By the end of this lesson you will generate a unique value per run, fill it into the
form, build a runtime XPath that *fails* and understand exactly why, build one that
*works*, and prove `text()` vs `normalize-space()` on real markup.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll build** | a value that differs every run, and an XPath assembled at runtime from it |
| **You'll prove** | why `@value` cannot find what you just typed — and what it *can* find |
| **Assumes** | [string building and Math.random()](/learn/w2/d3/p1) · [XPath syntax](/learn/w2/d2/p2) |
| **The idea worth keeping** | an HTML attribute and a live property are two different things |
> **Try it here**, with one real spec at the end.

## The problem with re-running the same test

| Rejected approach | Why |
|---|---|
| Delete the record after creating it | adds a second failure point — cleanup itself can fail |
| A file of pre-seeded data | runs out after N runs |
| `Date.now()` alone | two runs in the same second collide |

The fix from [Day 3.1](/learn/w2/d3/p1): `"prefix" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)`
— different every run, no file to run out of, nothing to clean up.

**Expected result:** the screenshot shows the field filled with a value starting
`learner...@example.com` — different characters every time you run the cell.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same idea, a different field: generate a unique phone number using digits only, with no `@example.com` on the end, and fill it into the `input[type='tel']` field. Getting this right now makes Problem 3 mostly typing.

blocks.text:
## Finding it again — the naive way, and why it fails

The obvious next move: build an XPath from that same string and locate the field by it.

**Expected (verified live):** `matches: 0`. `getAttribute('value')` prints `null`;
`inputValue()` prints the real string you filled.

HTML inputs keep two separate things: the **attribute** (`value="..."` in the original
markup — the default) and the **property** (what's actually in the box right now).
`.fill()` — and typing in general — only ever changes the property. XPath's `@value`
reads the attribute, which never moved. This is true of every plain `<input>`, not just
this app: **you cannot find a field by the value you just typed into it, via `@value`.**
If you need that value back, ask the locator you already have (`.inputValue()`), not XPath.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same proof, a different field: fill First Name with a generated value, then count `//input[@value='...']` for that value and print `.inputValue()` next to it. Confirm the count is 0 here too — so you know it is a rule about every plain `<input>`, not something peculiar to the email box.

blocks.text:
## A dynamic XPath that does work

`@value` matching works for anything whose value is **baked into the HTML markup** —
radio buttons and `<option>` tags, for example — because that attribute is part of the
page source, not something a script sets afterward. `Math.random()` can still decide
*which* one at runtime; you just can't invent an attribute value that was never there.

**Expected:** `matches: 1` and `checked: true`, whichever gender `Math.random()` picked
this run. Same string-building technique as the failing example — the difference is
entirely in what's really in the DOM, not in the XPath syntax.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same pattern, a different control: let `Math.random()` choose between the two checkbox ids you know (`#checkbox1` and `#checkbox2`), build the selector by concatenating the number onto `"#checkbox"`, then check it and print which one it picked.

blocks.text:
## `text()` vs `normalize-space()`

`text()` in XPath matches the exact text node — every leading, trailing, and internal
space included. Real markup is full of stray whitespace nobody notices.

**Expected (verified live):** raw text is `"Automation Demo Site "` — a real trailing
space baked into this app's markup, not a typo. `text()` finds **0**; `normalize-space()`
finds **1**. Default to `normalize-space()` whenever you match by text in XPath.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same two functions, the opposite direction: write the `text()` XPath that *does* match the heading, by putting the real trailing space inside your string. Then confirm `normalize-space()` still matches it as well. Both find it — and you will not want to maintain the first one.

blocks.text:
## Doing it for real, in a spec file

Unique email, dynamic-XPath gender pick, and a `normalize-space()` check, all in one test.

> ▶ **Run it yourself.** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day3-unique-data.spec.ts`
>
> Run it a second time immediately — it generates a different email and may pick the
> other gender, and still passes. That's the whole point of today.

## Best practices

- Build unique values with `+` and `Math.random()` — never a bare timestamp.
- Never assume `@value` finds what a user just typed — verify with `inputValue()` instead.
- Default to `normalize-space()` over `text()` for any XPath text match.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `//input[@value='...']` for a value you just `.fill()`ed | 0 matches, every time | use `.inputValue()`, or match on an attribute that's really in the markup |
| `//h1[text()='...']` against real markup | 0 matches when there's stray whitespace | use `normalize-space()` |
| A bare `Date.now()` as the "unique" value | two tests in the same second collide | concatenate `Math.random()` too |
You `.fill()` the email box with `learner7f3k2x@example.com`, then count `//input[@value='learner7f3k2x@example.com']`. How many matches?

options: 1 — the field holds exactly that value
0 — `@value` reads the markup attribute, which `.fill()` never touched
0, but only because the `@` in the email breaks the XPath
checkpoint.explanation: An `<input>` keeps two separate things: the `value="..."` **attribute** written in the markup, and the **property** holding what is in the box right now. `.fill()` and real typing change only the property. `getAttribute('value')` returns `null` here while `.inputValue()` returns your string. This is true of every plain `<input>`, not just this app.

blocks.text: So why does `//input[@value='FeMale']` find the gender radio perfectly well?

options: Because radios are exempt from the attribute-versus-property split
Because `FeMale` is written into the page source, so the attribute really is there
Because `.check()` writes the value attribute, unlike `.fill()`
checkpoint.explanation: A radio's `value` is part of the HTML the server sent — as is an `<option>`'s. Nothing at runtime had to set it, so `@value` finds it. `Math.random()` can still choose *which* one; what you cannot do is invent an attribute value that was never in the markup.

blocks.text: The heading's real text is `"Automation Demo Site "`. Which XPath matches it?

options: `//h1[text()='Automation Demo Site']`
`//h1[normalize-space()='Automation Demo Site']`
Both — XPath trims whitespace before comparing
checkpoint.explanation: `text()` matches the text node exactly, trailing space and all, so it finds 0. `normalize-space()` collapses the whitespace first and finds 1. Note this is the opposite of Playwright's own `toContainText`, which normalises for you — the normalisation you get depends on which tool is doing the matching.

blocks.text:
- Build unique values with `"prefix" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)`. A bare `Date.now()` collides when two runs land in the same second.
- **An attribute is not a property.** `@value` reads the markup; `.fill()` writes the live value. You cannot find a field by what you just typed into it.
- To read back what you typed, ask the locator you already have: `.inputValue()`.
- `@value` *does* work for values baked into the source — radios, `<option>` tags. Randomness picking which one is fine.
- Default to `normalize-space()` over `text()` for XPath text matching.

## What's next

[Day 3.3](/learn/w2/d3/p3) wraps unique-value generation and the working dynamic locator in a reusable function.

parts.title: Unique data and dynamic locators, wrapped for reuse

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - Implementation - Unique data and dynamic locators, wrapped for reuse

By the end of this lesson you will have a `uniqueEmail()` generator and a
`pickAndCheckGender()` helper that any spec can call, extending the same
`registration-helpers.ts` file from Days 1 and 2.

> **No new API here on purpose.** Everything below is something you already ran in [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2).

| | |
|---|---|
| **New API** | none — every line ran in [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2) |
| **What changes** | the random line and the dynamic-XPath line each move into a function, called instead of retyped |
| **Builds on** | the same `registration-helpers.ts` that Days [1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3) and [2.3](/learn/w2/d2/p3) have been growing |

## The problem with what we wrote yesterday

Every test that needs a unique value re-writes the same `Math.random()` line; every test
that needs a dynamic gender pick re-writes the same XPath-building line. Small lines, but
copy-pasted enough times they become the thing that's wrong when the pattern needs to change.

## Same code, with structure around it

| In Day 3.2 you wrote | Here it becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `"learner" + Math.random()...` inline | `uniqueEmail()` | one function that returns a fresh value; the "how" lives in exactly one place |
| the gender XPath built inline, then `.check()`ed | `pickAndCheckGender(page)` | the working dynamic-locator pattern, reusable without re-deriving it |

**Expected result:** `2 passed`. Both tests call `uniqueEmail()` independently and get
different strings — check the traces or add a `console.log` if you want to see both values.

## What a reviewer would look for

- The randomness lives inside `uniqueEmail()`, not copy-pasted into every test.
- `pickAndCheckGender` returns the choice it made, so a test can log or assert on it instead of guessing.
- Nothing here duplicates Day 3.2's logic — it's the same lines, moved once.
Two tests in the same file both call `uniqueEmail()`. Do they get the same string?

options: Yes — the module is loaded once, so the value is computed once and shared
No — the function body runs on each call, producing a fresh value each time
checkpoint.explanation: `uniqueEmail()` computes its value inside the function, so every call produces a new one. Had the randomness been assigned to a module-level `const` instead, both tests really would have shared it — and the collision this whole day exists to prevent would be back.

blocks.text: Why does `pickAndCheckGender(page)` return the choice it made, rather than just checking the radio and returning nothing?

options: So the caller can log or assert on which one was picked instead of guessing
Because an `async` function has to return something
So the next call knows which one to avoid
checkpoint.explanation: The function makes a random decision the test cannot otherwise see. Returning it hands that knowledge back to the caller, so a failure message can say which gender was picked. A helper that makes an invisible random choice is a helper you will be debugging blind.

blocks.text:
- Randomness belongs inside one generator function, not copy-pasted into every test that needs a fresh value.
- Compute the random value *inside* the function. A module-level `const` would be computed once and shared by every caller.
- A helper that makes a hidden decision should return it, so failures can say what it chose.
- These are the same lines from [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2), moved once — not rewritten.

## What's next

[Day 3.4](/learn/w2/d3/p4) — your turn, with no worked examples to lean on.

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - Practice - Unique data and dynamic locators

Three problems, getting harder. No answer key.

Write spec files into `week2/generated/` and run them with `npx playwright test`.

> Struggling for more than about twenty minutes on one problem means the gap is in
> [Day 3.1](/learn/w2/d3/p1) or [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2). Go back, re-read, come here again.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Three problems** | a unique value, then a dynamic locator over real `<option>` markup, then a generator of your own |
| **Pulls on** | [Day 3.1](/learn/w2/d3/p1) for the string building · [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2) for which attributes are real |
| **The question to keep asking** | is this attribute really in the page source, or did a script set it? |

## When you are done

Ask yourself the Day 3.2 question one more time: for any locator you wrote today, could
you swap in a value the site itself generated (not one you typed) and have it still work?
If the answer is "only via `@value`", check whether that attribute is really live markup
or something a script set — that's this week's whole lesson in one question.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Generate a unique First Name (e.g. `"Learner" + Math.random()...`),
fill it in, and assert it with `toHaveValue`.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `npx playwright test` passes, and running it twice in a row fills two different names — check the trace or a `console.log`.

**What to build.** Read every real `<option>` value out of `#Skills`, pick one at random
with `Math.random()`, build a dynamic XPath `//option[@value='...']` from that choice, and
assert it exists (`toHaveCount(1)`) before selecting it.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** The test passes on repeated runs even though it picks a different skill each time.

> **Hint** — [Day 3.2](/learn/w2/d3/p2) showed exactly this pattern for the gender radios; option `value`s are static markup too.

**What to build.** Add a `uniquePhone()` generator to
`week2/generated/registration-helpers.ts` (digits only — no `@example.com` suffix), then
a spec that fills the form twice with two different generated phone numbers and asserts
both values with `toHaveValue`.

**Where.** `week2/generated/registration-helpers.ts`, plus a spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `2 passed`, and the two asserted phone numbers are never the same.
